I hated hearing Jim say that; it made me think so much less of him. My conscience began troubling me worse than ever, until finally I told it, “Leave me alone—it isn’t too late. I’ll paddle ashore at the first light I see and tell on him.” Right away I felt peaceful and happy, light as a feather. Every worry disappeared. I began watching carefully for a light and singing a little to myself. After a while one appeared. Jim shouted:

“We’re safe, Huck, we’re safe! Jump up and kick your heels together! That’s good old Cairo at last—I just know it!”

I said:

“I’ll take the canoe and check, Jim. It might not be, you know.”

He jumped up and prepared the canoe, laid his old coat in the bottom for me to sit on, and handed me the paddle. As I pushed away, he said:

“Soon I’ll be shouting with joy, and I’ll say it’s all thanks to Huck. I’m a free man, and I never could have been free without Huck. Huck did it. Jim will never forget you, Huck. You’re the best friend Jim ever had, and you’re the only friend old Jim has now.”

I was paddling away, all worked up and eager to report him. But those words seemed to drain all the strength out of me. I slowed down, no longer sure whether I was glad I had set off. When I was fifty yards away, Jim called:

“There goes faithful old Huck—the only white gentleman who ever kept a promise to old Jim.”

Well, I felt sick. But I told myself I had to do it; there was no way out. Just then a small boat came along with two men carrying guns. They stopped, and so did I. One asked:

“What’s that over there?”

“Part of a raft,” I said.

“Are you travelling on it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Any men aboard?”

“Just one, sir.”

“Well, five slaves ran away tonight from up there, above the bend. Is your man white or Black?”

I didn’t answer straight away. I tried, but no words came. For a second or two I tried to summon the courage to say it, but I wasn’t man enough. I didn’t have a rabbit’s nerve. I could feel myself weakening, so I stopped trying and said:

“He’s white.”

“I think we’ll go and look for ourselves.”

“I wish you would,” I said, “because it’s my father over there, and maybe you could help me tow the raft ashore to that light.

“No, no, that’s tomorrow, and for that very reason I particularly wanted to see Knightley today. Such a terribly scorching morning! I walked across the fields too”—his tone conveyed a strong sense of mistreatment—“which made it much worse. And then to discover he wasn’t home! I assure you I am far from pleased. No apology left, no message for me. The housekeeper insisted she knew nothing about my being expected. Quite extraordinary! And nobody had any idea where he had gone. Perhaps to Hartfield, perhaps to Abbey Mill, perhaps into his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is unlike our friend Knightley! Can you explain it?”

Emma entertained herself by agreeing that it was extraordinary indeed and declaring that she could not say a word in his defence.

“I cannot imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, feeling the insult as a wife ought, “I simply cannot imagine how he could treat you this way, of all people! The very last person anyone should expect him to forget! My dear Mr. E., he must have left a message; I’m certain he did. Even Knightley couldn’t be quite so eccentric. His servants must have forgotten it. Depend on it, that is what happened—and it’s very likely with the Donwell servants, whom I have often noticed to be extremely clumsy and careless. Nothing would persuade me to let a creature like his Harry serve at our sideboard. As for Mrs. Hodges, Wright has a very low opinion of her. She promised Wright a recipe and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins,” Mr. Elton continued, “as I approached the house. He told me I wouldn’t find his master home, but I didn’t believe him. William seemed rather out of sorts. He said he didn’t know what had come over his master lately, but he could hardly ever manage to speak to him. William’s needs are no concern of mine, but it really is extremely important that I see Knightley today. Having made this hot walk for nothing is therefore a very serious inconvenience.”

Emma felt that her best course was to go home immediately. In all likelihood, someone was waiting for her there at that very moment; and she might save Mr. Knightley from offending Mr. Elton still further, even if she could do nothing for William Larkins.

As she took her leave, she was pleased to discover that Miss Fairfax was determined to accompany her out of the room and even downstairs. This gave her an opportunity, which she immediately used, to say,

“Oh, I mistook your meaning. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ and naturally supposed ‘anybody’ meant—well, anybody; everybody, in fact.”

“It doth—any person of noble birth; and royalty is better yet.”

“That seems to me entirely fitting,” said the abbot, perceiving a chance to restore harmony and ward off disaster, “for surely so marvellous a power would not be bestowed to disclose the affairs of beings less exalted than those born near the heights of greatness. Our king Arthur—”

“Would you hear news of him?” the enchanter interrupted.

“Most willingly, yes, and with gratitude.”

At once they all became awestruck and interested again, the hopeless fools. They followed the incantations with rapt attention, and when the announcement came, their glances at me plainly said, “There! What have you to say now?”

“The king, exhausted by the hunt, hath lain these two hours in his palace, wrapped in dreamless sleep.”

“God bless him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May his slumber renew both body and soul.”

“So it might, if he were asleep,” I replied, “but the king isn’t asleep. He’s riding.”

There was trouble once more—two authorities contradicting each other. Nobody knew whom to trust, for I still possessed a little credit. The magician’s contempt was aroused, and he said:

“Behold, in all my days I have encountered many extraordinary prophets, seers, and magicians, yet never one who could sit doing nothing and penetrate the heart of matters without a single incantation.”

“You’ve spent your life in the woods and missed a great deal. I employ incantations too, as these good brothers know—but only for important occasions.”

When sarcasm is called for, I believe I can hold my own. That thrust made the fellow wriggle. The abbot asked about the queen and her court, receiving this answer:

“They likewise sleep, overcome with weariness, even as the king.”

I answered:

“That’s simply one more lie. Half are enjoying their amusements; the queen and the remaining half are riding, not sleeping. Now perhaps you can exert yourself a little and inform us where the king, queen, and everyone riding with them at this moment are headed?”

“As I have said, they now sleep; tomorrow they shall ride, being bound on a journey toward the sea.”

“And where will they be at vespers the day after tomorrow?”

“Far northward of Camelot, with half their journey accomplished.”

“There’s another lie, to the extent of a hundred and fifty miles.
